We are six third-year female Computer Engineering students from Türkiye, united by our passion for technology, science, and space exploration. We aim to combine NASA's open data, artificial intelligence, and creative problem-solving to develop innovative solutions. We believe in teamwork, curiosity, and the power of women in STEM.

Six women. One team. Infinite possibilities! 🚀✨
summary: Analog Atlas is an offline regional pre-screening and decision-support application that identifies Earth regions matching selected Mars and Moon environmental conditions and evaluates each selected region's potential to retain those target conditions in future periods. Rather than reducing similarity to a single opaque score, it lets researchers define bounds, priorities, and mandatory filters across 11 measurable climate, surface, and geological parameters—or start from six Mars and Moon scenarios—while transparently showing per-parameter breakdowns, documented analog sites, and explicit scientific limitations. Our core added value lies in applying dedicated suitability-scoring, spatial-clustering, and scenario-based climate projection algorithms to open NASA and global datasets to generate future projections that reveal how the similarity rate of desired Earth locations to Mars and Moon surface conditions may shift over time. By also evaluating relative surface-process trends to make these selection outcomes sustainable, Analog Atlas helps planetary scientists choose resilient Earth test sites for long-term exploration research.
details:
Analog Atlas

Analog Atlas is designed to help users identify and evaluate potential planetary analog sites through a four-step process: Target, Suitable Regions, Future Climate, and Report. The workflow brings together complex scientific datasets in an accessible interface, while keeping data preparation separate from the browser-based analysis. Once downloaded, the tool can be used entirely offline.

How the Tool Works

Offline Grid Construction

Before the application is built, global datasets are processed and aligned to a common terrestrial grid with a resolution of 0.5°. This produces 95,447 land cells containing 66 numerical variables. To keep the application lightweight and portable, the data are converted into 16-bit integers, compressed using gzip, and encoded in Base64. The resulting dataset occupies approximately 8 MB and is embedded directly into a single HTML file, bringing the complete application size to around 14.7 MB.

Configurable Multi-Parameter Scoring

Users can start with one of six predefined target profiles, including four designed for Mars and two for the Moon, or create their own criteria. Each profile can be adjusted by setting parameter ranges, assigning weights between 0 and 3, excluding ice-covered areas, and defining mandatory filters.

The scoring system considers 11 parameters: temperature, precipitation, aridity (P/PET), diurnal temperature range (DTR), freeze-thaw days, permafrost indicator, wind speed, bare surface fraction, elevation, terrain relief, and lithology. This allows users to evaluate candidate regions according to the environmental conditions most relevant to their research.

Similarity Analysis and Regional Identification

For each parameter, the tool calculates how closely a location matches the selected target conditions. When a value falls outside the specified range, its contribution to the overall score gradually decreases according to a Gaussian function. Precipitation and aridity are handled using logarithmic scaling to better account for their distribution.

After scoring, the application identifies promising areas using a dynamic threshold based on the top 2% of scores and a minimum score of 0.70. Neighboring cells are then grouped into regions using an 8-neighbor depth-first search algorithm, with longitudinal wrap-around to account for the continuity of the global map.

The resulting regions are assigned names based on Natural Earth geographic data and can be compared with 31 analog sites documented in scientific literature.

Future Climate and Reusability Analysis

One of the main features of Analog Atlas is its ability to examine whether a candidate region is likely to retain its suitability under future climate conditions.

For each selected region, the tool evaluates 18 climate projection combinations. These combine three CMIP6 climate models (IPSL-CM6A-LR, MPI-ESM1-2-HR, and MRI-ESM2-0), two emissions scenarios (SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5), and three future periods: 2021–2040, 2041–2060, and 2061–2080.

Future climate variables are calculated using the Delta method. Potential evapotranspiration is estimated with the FAO-56 Hargreaves method, while freeze-thaw conditions are derived from temperature data.

Rather than evaluating a location only according to its present-day conditions, this analysis provides a way to investigate how its suitability may change over several decades.

Surface Indicators and Report Generation

The application also recalculates climate suitability for future periods using the original target criteria. In addition, it includes five experimental indicators related to surface processes: chemical weathering, freeze-thaw fracturing, water-related processes, wind-related processes, and a composite landform-change indicator.

Changes in UNEP soil regimes are also included to provide further context for interpreting future environmental conditions.

Once the analysis is complete, users can generate reports in printable PDF or text format. These reports bring together the selected criteria, regional scores, climate projections, and relevant scientific notes.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Comparing global climate, land-cover, geological, and political boundary datasets often requires working with multiple sources and performing a considerable amount of manual processing. This can make the analysis time-consuming and difficult to reproduce.

Analog Atlas addresses this problem by bringing these datasets together in a single application that does not require a server, paid API, or continuous internet connection. All calculations and visualizations run directly in a modern web browser after the initial download.

The tool is intended to support planetary scientists, mission planners, and astrobiology researchers during the early stages of site selection. By combining present-day environmental similarity with future climate projections, it offers a more comprehensive way to assess potential analog locations.

An important part of this approach is considering long-term suitability before making significant investments in field research. A location that closely matches the desired conditions today may become less suitable in the future. Analog Atlas helps researchers identify this possibility earlier in the selection process.

Tools, Programming Languages, Software, and Data Sources

Data Processing and Application Build

The data preparation pipeline was developed in Python, using NumPy, SciPy, Shapely (including STRtree spatial indexing), Rasterio, and Pillow.

Frontend and Visualization

The browser-based application was built with HTML5, CSS, and Vanilla JavaScript. D3.js and TopoJSON Client are used for geographic data handling and visualization, while HTML Canvas supports interactive mapping. Plotly.js is used to display climate ensemble charts.

The application also relies on the browser's native DecompressionStream API to handle compressed data. Reporting and data export are supported through the browser's print-to-PDF and clipboard capabilities.

Testing and Verification

To verify that the scoring system produces consistent results, calculations were compared across Python and JavaScript using 5,880 identical test cases.

The interface was also tested automatically with Chromium and Playwright. All 22 test cases passed, covering offline functionality, predefined profiles, input validation, maps, charts, report generation, keyboard navigation, and responsive layouts.

Scientific Datasets

The project uses the following datasets:

  • NASA MODIS MCD12 IGBP Land Cover: 2023 land-cover data accessed through NASA GIBS.
  • WorldClim v2.1: Historical climate reference data covering 1970–2000.
  • WorldClim CMIP6: Future climate projections.
  • GLiM: Global lithological data at 0.5° resolution.
  • Natural Earth: Geographic boundaries at 1:50m scale.
  • Scientific Literature: 31 documented planetary analog sites used for comparison.

What Makes Analog Atlas Different?

Looking Beyond Present-Day Suitability

A common limitation of analog site selection is treating suitable locations as if their environmental conditions were permanent. Analog Atlas takes a different approach by examining how well a region may retain its selected characteristics under different climate models and emissions scenarios through 2080.

This makes long-term climate resilience part of the site selection process rather than an afterthought.

Transparent and Explainable Results

The tool does not rely on a single unexplained similarity score. Users can inspect individual parameter contributions, see how mandatory filters affect the results, compare the spread between three climate models, and review missing-data counts.

Methodological notes are also provided to make the assumptions and limitations behind the calculations easier to understand. This gives researchers a clearer picture of why a region receives a particular score and where potential uncertainties lie.

A Portable, Single-File Application

Another distinguishing feature is the application's architecture. By combining binary quantization, compression, and embedded datasets, Analog Atlas stores 95,447 global land cells and 66 variables in a self-contained HTML file.

There is no need to install a separate backend, connect to a remote server, purchase API access, or maintain an internet connection during use. This makes the tool easier to distribute, access, and reproduce across different research environments.

Scientific Considerations and Limitations

Resolution and Regional Screening

The application uses a 0.5° grid, corresponding to approximately 55.6 km multiplied by cos(latitude) in the east-west direction. This resolution is suitable for broad global comparisons, but it can overlook smaller geological formations and local surface variations.

For this reason, Analog Atlas should be considered an initial screening tool rather than a substitute for detailed fieldwork or local geotechnical assessment.

Differences Between Earth and Other Planetary Environments

A similarity score of 100/100 means that a location fully matches the selected terrestrial criteria. It does not mean that the location is an exact replica of Mars or the Moon.

Fundamental differences such as gravity, the thin or nearly absent atmospheres of other planetary bodies, and exposure to space radiation cannot be reproduced naturally on Earth. These factors remain outside the scope of the scoring system.

Future Climate Data and Missing Variables

Not all environmental variables are updated in the future climate analysis. Six climate-dependent variables are recalculated using CMIP6 projections, while wind speed, bare surface fraction, elevation, terrain relief, and lithology are kept constant.

For future reusability analysis, the application also relaxes the original mandatory filters. This is intentional: it allows users to observe how conditions gradually move away from the initial target rather than excluding a region as soon as it no longer satisfies a strict filter.

Some grid cells have no available CMIP6 data for particular models or periods. These gaps are explicitly reported rather than silently ignored. For example, 6,138 of the 95,447 land cells lack temperature coverage for SSP2-4.5 during 2061–2080.

Reference Periods and Experimental Indicators

The datasets used in the project do not all represent the same time period. Historical climate normals cover 1970–2000, whereas the MODIS land-cover dataset represents 2023. They are therefore treated as reference baselines, not as synchronized or real-time observations.

The five surface-process indicators are also experimental relative indices. They should not be interpreted as calibrated erosion measurements or direct alternatives to established models such as RUSLE and RWEQ.

Similarly, agreement between climate models suggests consistency in the projected direction of change, but it should not be interpreted as a measure of statistical confidence.

These limitations are important when interpreting the results and are deliberately made visible so that users can evaluate the findings within their appropriate scientific context.
